title: Ring invariance of normalized local pairs, branch count and defect length
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $H,H'$ be nonzero reduced commutative Noetherian local $k$-algebras, with residue fields identified with $k$ by their structural maps [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]; reduced means having no nonzero nilpotent. For a reduced ring $R$ write $Q(R)$ for its localization at the non-zero-divisors (those $s$ for which $sr=0$ forces $r=0$), and $\overline R$ for the integral closure of $R$ in $Q(R)$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Assume $\overline H$ and $\overline {H'}$ are finite over their respective rings [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], that $\overline H/H$ and $\overline {H'}/H'$ are finite-dimensional over $k$, and that
$$\overline H\cong\prod_{i=1}^b S_i,\qquad \overline {H'}\cong\prod_{j=1}^{b'} S'_j$$
for finite nonempty families of nonzero local integral domains. Every ring isomorphism $\varphi:H\cong H'$ extends uniquely to a ring isomorphism $Q(H)\cong Q(H')$, carries $\overline H$ onto $\overline {H'}$, and induces an additive isomorphism of quotients satisfying $\overline\varphi(hm)=\varphi(h)\overline\varphi(m)$. It identifies their lattices of submodules, their finite composition lengths [def-weil-pbc-module-length], and their sets of primitive nonzero idempotents (idempotents not expressible as the sum of two nonzero orthogonal idempotents) in the integral closures. Consequently $b=b'$ and
$$\dim_k(\overline H/H)=\operatorname{length}_H(\overline H/H)=\operatorname{length}_{H'}(\overline {H'}/H')=\dim_k(\overline {H'}/H').$$
If $\varphi$ is a $k$-algebra isomorphism, its extensions and quotient isomorphism are also $k$-linear. No scalar compatibility of $\varphi$ is required for the equality of lengths, dimensions, or branch counts.

source.place: Agent-written ring-invariance comparison needed to use the normalization and delta computation in Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross) with the ring-isomorphism definition of a node; integral closure means algebra.tex Tag 00GP (definition-integral-closure). Expands returned proof steps 9 and 11, without assuming a ring isomorphism is k-linear.

proof.text: The non-zero-divisors form a multiplicative set: $1x=0$ implies $x=0$, and $stx=0$ implies $tx=0$ and then $x=0$. If $s$ is a non-zero-divisor of $H$ and $\varphi(s)y=0$, write $y=\varphi(x)$; injectivity gives $sx=0$, hence $y=0$. Apply this also to $\varphi^{-1}$, so $\varphi$ bijects the denominator sets. The localization universal property applied to $H\xrightarrow{\varphi}H'\to Q(H')$ gives $F:Q(H)\to Q(H')$, with $F(a/s)=\varphi(a)/\varphi(s)$. Applying it to the inverse gives $G$; $GF$ and $FG$ agree with the identities on the base rings, so uniqueness makes them identities. The same uniqueness proves uniqueness of $F$. We regard $H$ as a subring of $Q(H)$: $a/1=0$ means $sa=0$ for a denominator $s$, hence $a=0$; similarly for $H'$.

source.place: Tag 00CP (proposition-universal-property-localization), and the injectivity observation immediately preceding it; explicit denominator check for the present isomorphism.

proof.text: For $z\in\overline H$, choose a monic equation $z^n+\sum_{i<n}a_i z^i=0$ with $a_i\in H$. Applying $F$ gives $F(z)^n+\sum_{i<n}\varphi(a_i)F(z)^i=0$, so $F(z)\in\overline {H'}$. The identical calculation for $G$ proves the reverse inclusion. Thus $E=F|_{\overline H}:\overline H\to\overline {H'}$ is a ring isomorphism with inverse $G|_{\overline {H'}}$, and $E(h)=\varphi(h)$ on $H$.

source.place: Tag 00GP (definition-integral-closure), using the monic-equation definition of integrality (Tag 00GI).

proof.text: Put $M=\overline H/H$ and $M'=\overline {H'}/H'$, as additive module quotients. Define $T:M\to M'$ by $T([z])=[E(z)]$. Replacing $z$ by $z+h$ changes $E(z)$ by $\varphi(h)\in H'$, so this is well-defined. It is additive, and $[w]\mapsto[E^{-1}(w)]$ is its inverse by the same check. For $h\in H$, $T(h[z])=[E(hz)]=[\varphi(h)E(z)]=\varphi(h)T([z])$. The inverse satisfies the corresponding identity with $\varphi^{-1}$.

source.place: Agent calculation with the integral-closure pair of Tag 00GP; application to the normalization defect in curves.tex Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross).

proof.text: For an $H$-submodule $N\subseteq M$, the additive subgroup $T(N)$ is an $H'$-submodule: given $h'\in H'$ and $T(x)\in T(N)$, set $h=\varphi^{-1}(h')$ and use $h'T(x)=T(hx)$. Applying $T^{-1}$ gives the inverse correspondence. Both maps preserve inclusion, so this is an order isomorphism of submodule lattices; consequently it also preserves their meets and joins, characterized as greatest lower and least upper bounds. It bijects strict chains and their lengths, including their zero and whole-module endpoints, so the definition of length gives $\operatorname{length}_H M=\operatorname{length}_{H'}M'$. The same image/preimage argument using $E(hz)=\varphi(h)E(z)$ identifies the submodule lattices of the two integral closures as well.

source.place: Tag 02LY (definition-length); direct submodule-chain argument, analogous to Tag 00IX (lemma-length-independent) but allowing a semilinear bijection.

proof.text: Every $H$-submodule of $M$ is a $k$-linear subspace because the $k$-action factors through $H$. Along a strict submodule chain its $k$-dimension strictly increases, so all chain lengths are at most $\dim_k M<\infty$. Thus $M$ has finite $H$-length. The cited simple-filtration theorem gives $0=M_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_r=M$ with nonzero simple factors $V_i=M_i/M_{i-1}$. These subquotients retain their compatible $k$-vector-space structures and are finite-dimensional. Apply the same argument separately to $H'$ and $M'$, using its own structural $k$-action. When a defect is zero its filtration has $r=0$.

Fix a factor $V_i$ from Step 5 and $0
e v\in V_i$. Simplicity says $Hv=V_i$. The surjection $H	o V_i$, $a\mapsto av$, has proper kernel $I$. If $I\subsetneq J\subsetneq H$ were an ideal, its image $Jv$ would be a nonzero proper submodule: it is nonzero since some $a\in J\setminus I$ has $av
e0$, and $Jv=V_i$ would give $1-j\in I\subset J$ for some $j\in J$, contradicting $J
e H$. Thus $I$ is maximal, and locality gives $I=\mathfrak m_H$. The map $H/I	o V_i$, $a+I\mapsto av$, is bijective and $k$-linear. The structural residue-field identification $k	o H/\mathfrak m_H$ is a $k$-linear bijection; hence $\dim_k V_i=1$. Its only submodules are $0,V_i$, so its length is $1$ by the chain definition. This calculation applies to every factor for $H'$ as well, with its own maximal ideal and structural residue map.

source.place: Tag 00J2 (lemma-characterize-length-1), cyclic-generator argument written out; locality and the structural residue-field hypothesis identify the quotient with k.

proof.text: The inclusion and quotient maps give short exact sequences $0\to M_{i-1}\to M_i\to V_i\to0$. Additivity of module length yields inductively $\operatorname{length}_H M_i=i$, starting with the zero module of length $0$ and using Step 6. The same sequences of finite-dimensional $k$-spaces give $\dim_k M_i=i$: extend a basis of $M_{i-1}$ by a lift of a basis of the one-dimensional quotient $V_i$. Therefore $\dim_k M=r=\operatorname{length}_H M$. Repeating for $M'$ gives $\dim_k M'=\operatorname{length}_{H'}M'$. Combine these equalities with Step 4 to obtain all four equal quantities in the statement. No equality of the two structural maps from $k$ has entered this argument.

source.place: Tag 00IV (lemma-length-additive); finite iteration on the filtration of Tag 00J3, with elementary basis extension for vector-space dimensions.

proof.text: A ring isomorphism preserves and reflects the equations $e^2=e$, $ef=0$, $e=f+g$, and nonzeroness. Thus $E$ and $E^{-1}$ biject primitive nonzero idempotents: any forbidden orthogonal decomposition on either side pulls back or pushes forward to one on the other. In $\prod_{i=1}^b S_i$, every idempotent coordinate satisfies $e_i(e_i-1)=0$, hence is $0$ or $1$ because $S_i$ is a domain. Its support is therefore a subset of $\{1,\ldots,b\}$. A nonempty support of size at least two splits into two nonempty disjoint supports, giving a decomposition into nonzero orthogonal idempotents. A singleton support cannot so split, since orthogonality makes the two supports disjoint and their union the singleton. Consequently the primitive nonzero idempotents are exactly the $b$ coordinate idempotents. The same calculation gives $b'$ on the other side, whence $b=b'$.

source.place: Agent coordinate calculation for the product-normalization setting of curves.tex Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross).

proof.text: Finally suppose $\varphi$ is a $k$-algebra isomorphism. For $c\in k$, $F(c)=\varphi(c)=c$, so $F(cx)=cF(x)$ in the total fraction rings. Its restriction $E$ and the induced map $T$ have the same scalar identity, as do their inverses. Thus they are $k$-linear. Without this extra assumption Step 3 supplies precisely the $\varphi$-semilinear identity, and Steps 4, 7, and 8 already give the length, dimension, and branch-count equalities.
